title: May I Use the Copier, Because...
text:
In the 1970s, the psychologist Ellen Langer and her colleagues Arthur Blank and Benzion Chanowitz ran a quiet experiment at a library copy machine at the City University of New York. A researcher waited until someone was about to make copies, then asked to cut in line. The wording was varied.

With a plain request ("Excuse me, I have five pages. May I use the Xerox machine?"), about 60 percent of people let the researcher go first. With a real reason ("because I'm in a rush"), about 94 percent agreed. The surprise came with a reason that contained no information at all: "May I use the Xerox machine, because I have to make copies?" Of course she had to make copies. Yet about 93 percent agreed, almost exactly as many as with the real reason.

The trick worked only when the stakes were small. When the researcher asked to copy twenty pages, the empty reason helped no more than no reason, while the real reason still did. Langer argued that for small requests people respond to the familiar shape of a request with "because" and do not really process what follows. When the cost goes up, they start paying attention.
lesson: Giving a reason makes people far more willing to help. For anything that matters, make it a real reason, since people stop accepting empty ones when the cost goes up.
people: Ellen Langer, Arthur Blank, Benzion Chanowitz
location: City University of New York, New York, USA
source: Langer, E., Blank, A., and Chanowitz, B. (1978). The mindlessness of ostensibly thoughtful action: The role of 'placebic' information in interpersonal interaction. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 36(6), 635-642.
